B1:
Touched fires many times: once for every body part (feet, legs, HumanoidRootPart) and repeatedly while they overlap. Destroy only takes effect after the current events, so several handlers run before the part is gone, and each one adds 10. Fix it with a server-side debounce or claimed flag that is set before granting:
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local claimed = false
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
  if claimed then return end
  local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
  if not plr then return end
  local coins = plr:FindFirstChild('leaderstats') and plr.leaderstats:FindFirstChild('Coins')
  if not coins then return end
  claimed = true
  coins.Value += 10
  part:Destroy()
end)
```
For a reusable pickup, use a per-player cooldown table and clean it up.
B2: With StreamingEnabled the client only has parts near the player. Distant buildings or doors haven't streamed in yet (or have streamed out), so indexing workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel.Door with dot syntax errors when the LocalScript runs. Fix 1: wait for it, for example local door = workspace.Map:WaitForChild('Buildings'):WaitForChild('Hotel'):WaitForChild('Door', 10) with a timeout and nil check. Better, set the Hotel or Door model's ModelStreamingMode to Atomic (or Persistent if it must always exist) so one WaitForChild is enough. Fix 2: drive it by tags. Tag doors 'Door' and use CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal('Door') plus GetTagged to connect Touched when each door streams in, and disconnect on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. Also consider handling door touches on the server, where everything exists.
B3: Bugs: (1) It returns PurchaseGranted even when pcall failed, so the player is charged and gets nothing. (2) There is no idempotency or PurchaseId record, so Roblox retries (timeouts, or a save that actually went through) grant the coins again. (3) GetAsync followed by SetAsync isn't atomic, so concurrent writes overwrite each other. (4) plr can be nil if the player has left, and plr.UserId errors (use info.PlayerId). (5) It writes to a separate store that may disagree with the live session data. Correct behaviour: find the player, and return NotProcessedYet if they are absent or their data isn't loaded. In one UpdateAsync (or a session-locked profile), if data.receipts[info.PurchaseId] already exists, return it unchanged. Otherwise add the coins and record the PurchaseId. Return PurchaseGranted only if the write succeeded, otherwise NotProcessedYet. Update the in-game coins after the save. Keep only one ProcessReceipt in the game.
B4: Remote arguments are serialized. Tables are sent as plain data, and metatables and functions are stripped, so the client gets {Name='Rifle', Ammo=30} without the Weapon metatable and w:Fire is nil. Instances are sent as references, but the client can't see anything in ServerStorage (it never replicates), so the reference arrives as nil. Fixes: send plain data (for example an id or {Name, Ammo}) and rebuild the object on the client with a shared ModuleScript class in ReplicatedStorage: setmetatable(data, Weapon). Move Muzzle to ReplicatedStorage or workspace (somewhere replicated) before sending it, or send an identifier the client can resolve, or clone it into a replicated location first.
B5:
The second argument to workspace:Raycast is the direction vector including its length, and .Unit gives a 1-stud ray, so it almost never reaches the target. Use a length: local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 500 (or just target - origin, plus a bit). Also exclude the shooter with RaycastParams:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, (target - origin).Unit * 500, params)
if r then print(r.Instance) end
```
Otherwise the ray can hit the gun or the shooter's own body first.
B6: When the last player leaves, the server starts shutting down, and PlayerRemoving's yielding SetAsync can be killed before it finishes. A server shutdown (or update) can also close without PlayerRemoving saves completing. The standard fix is game:BindToClose: when the server closes, save every remaining player's data in parallel (task.spawn per player, then wait for all of them) within the roughly 30-second limit. Use UpdateAsync with retries, and avoid double-saving with a per-player 'saving' flag. Also autosave periodically so a crash loses little. In Studio, BindToClose can just wait briefly when RunService:IsStudio().

```lua
local lastUse = {} -- [Player] = time

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, ...)
```

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService('TweenService')
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
local OPEN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)

local function close()
  if current then current:Cancel() end
  local t = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = CLOSED})
  current = t
  t.Completed:Connect(function(state)

  end)
  t:Play()
end
```
The menu is hidden only after the slide-out finishes, and a canceled close (reopened mid-tween) doesn't hide it.

```lua
local MAX_RANGE, DAMAGE = 200, 20

local function shoot(player: Player, targetPos: Vector3)
  if typeof(targetPos) ~= 'Vector3' or targetPos ~= targetPos then return end
  local char = player.Character
  local head = char and char:FindFirstChild('Head')
  local myHum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass('Humanoid')
```

```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService('CollectionService')
local TAG = 'KillBrick'
local conns = {} -- [part] = connection

CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(onRemoved)
```

B13: (a) Use a RemoteEvent (or a client-to-server RemoteFunction if the UI needs an immediate success/failure result) for client to server: BuySword(itemId). The client only sends a request. Validation, prices and the coin balance all live on the server (server data, mirrored to leaderstats or attributes). The server checks the item exists, the price comes from the server catalog, the balance is enough, and rate limits, then deducts and grants. (b) For the server-to-client update, use a RemoteEvent FireClient (CoinsChanged) or just replicate the value through leaderstats/IntValue/attributes, and have the client listen with .Changed or GetAttributeChangedSignal. Never use RemoteFunction:InvokeClient for this: the server yields until the client replies, an exploiter can never respond (hanging the server thread forever) or throw errors, and if the client leaves it errors. That's a server-thread hang and DoS risk for no benefit, since the UI needs no reply.
B14: Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData) travels with the client and can be read or spoofed by the client, it isn't guaranteed (failed teleports, joining directly), and it has size limits. It's fine for non-authoritative hints like the chosen map, party id or a UI preference, but never for coins. DataStores are authoritative and persistent: save the balance and loadout (with session lock released) before teleporting, then load them in the match place. MemoryStores are fast and short-lived (TTL): good for a server-written 'ticket' or match handoff, such as the loadout chosen for this match, keyed by userId, with expiry about 5 minutes. My choice: coins stay in the DataStore player profile, saved and released before TeleportAsync, then loaded with the session lock in the match place. The chosen loadout goes in a server-written MemoryStore entry (or the profile), validated against what the player owns. Teleport data is used only for non-trusted hints like the match id. Validate everything on arrival.
B15: Giving 610 instances their own Script means 610 copies of code. It's hard to update or fix (copies drift), uses more memory and startup work and more threads and connections, makes cleanup inconsistent, and copies are easy to miss or duplicate. A tag-driven architecture tags instances ('Door', 'Pickup', 'Turret') with CollectionService. One server Script/module per tag (a service) runs setup and teardown for every tagged instance and keeps per-instance state in a table keyed by instance. Use config from attributes (for example Damage or Range), and drive turrets from one central loop/Heartbeat with a budget instead of 60 loops. Structure: ServerScriptService/Services/DoorService, PickupService, TurretService, plus client-side tag modules for visuals. Handling new instances: connect GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag) and also iterate GetTagged(tag) for existing ones, and make setup idempotent. Clean up connections and state on GetInstanceRemovedSignal (which also fires on Destroy or, on clients, streaming out). Spawned clones keep their tags. With StreamingEnabled, client code only reacts to added/removed, so streamed-in doors work automatically, and server logic stays authoritative.
B16: Give the driver network ownership of the car while seated (VehicleSeat occupant changes, so call SetNetworkOwner(driver) on the car's assembly). This gives responsive, lag-free physics for the driver. When they exit, return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) and keep parked or empty cars server-owned or anchored. The risk is that the owning client simulates the physics and the server accepts it, so an exploiter can teleport the car, speed-hack, fly, noclip, fling other players, or fake lap and checkpoint progress. The server must still validate speed and acceleration (max per car type, with tolerance), the position delta per tick and teleports, staying on the track or ground, checkpoint order and timing (lap times above the minimum possible), and collisions or flings on others. It should handle all lap, finish, reward and damage logic, and use strike counts and reset rather than instant kicks. For competitive racing, consider Server Authority mode (2026), which uses server simulation with client prediction instead of client ownership.
B17: Use an UnreliableRemoteEvent for the aim/position stream, since only the latest value matters, and send less: about 10-20 Hz or only when the change exceeds a threshold, with compressed payloads. Constraints: the payload is limited to about 1,000 bytes per send (larger sends are dropped), and there's no ordering or delivery guarantee: packets can be dropped or arrive out of order, and are dropped under congestion, throttling or with no handler. Handling: include a sequence number or timestamp and discard stale packets. Make every message self-contained (absolute state, not deltas). Quantize the data (for example a direction as two angles in int16s, packed in a buffer) to stay small. Interpolate or extrapolate on receivers to hide gaps. Keep important events (fire, hit, reload, state changes) on a reliable RemoteEvent, because a lost unreliable packet would leave things stuck. Still validate and rate-limit on the server. Also, character position already replicates through physics, so you don't need to send it.
B18: Split the NPCs across several Actors (for example 8-16 Actors with about 12-25 NPCs each, or one script per Actor driving a batch), not one Actor, which gives no speed-up. In each Actor, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run raycasts and path scoring in parallel. workspace:Raycast and reading properties are allowed in parallel. Then call task.synchronize() (or queue the results) to apply the writes, like moving NPCs, setting properties, Humanoid:MoveTo and firing remotes, in the serial phase. Limitations: most instance property writes, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs aren't allowed while desynchronized. Each Actor has its own Luau VM, so module state isn't shared. Communicate through Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage (arguments are copied, so send ids, not big tables) or SharedTable (for shared data, with atomic update/increment). Require modules at load time. Parallel results only apply at the sync point (a one-frame delay). Also cut the work: spread NPC updates over several frames, lower the update rate for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile in the MicroProfiler Threads view first.
B19: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Settings: StreamingMinRadius around 64 (the default; larger, for example 128-256, for fast movement or arenas), StreamingTargetRadius around 256-1024 (keep it moderate for mobile memory), StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic (or LowMemory), and StreamingIntegrityMode = PauseOutsideLoadedArea or MinimumRadiusPause, so players don't fall into unloaded areas. Per model: ModelStreamingMode = Atomic for interactables or multipart objects that must arrive whole, Persistent only for the few things that must always exist (keep it rare), and PersistentPerPlayer for a player's own vehicle or base. Use Model LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant imposters. Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleports or spawns. Scripts: client scripts can no longer assume something exists. Replace direct indexing with WaitForChild (with timeouts) on Atomic models, or better, use CollectionService tags with GetInstanceAddedSignal/RemovedSignal so setup runs when content streams in and cleans up when it streams out. Handle nil and parts disappearing. Keep authoritative logic on the server, which has everything. Test with Studio's streaming emulation and on a low-end device.
B20: 80 players saving every 5 s is about 960 writes per minute. That exceeds the write budget (300 + 20 x CCU, about 1,900/min shared, and the per-key limit allows only about 1 write per 6 s), and the per-server request queues fill up, so requests are throttled or dropped ('queue full', 302) and saves are lost. Repeated SetAsync to the same key also hits the per-key write cooldown. Better design: keep data in memory per session, with a dirty flag. Autosave each player every 60-180 s, staggered with a random offset per player and jitter, skipping clean data. Use UpdateAsync with session locking. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (in parallel), and immediately only on important events like purchases. On failure, retry with exponential backoff, never in a tight loop. Watch DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving, and log the budget. Merge changes into one write per player rather than several keys.
B21: In Roblox Studio, open the Assistant panel's settings (the '...' menu / Manage MCP Servers, under Assistant or Studio settings) and turn on 'Enable Studio as MCP server'. Then add Studio as an MCP server in the external client (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI). It's built in since the September 2025 Assistant update, replacing the old community server, which was archived in April 2026. Tools include execute_luau, get_console_output, start_stop_play, get_studio_state, list_roblox_studios, script_read, script_grep, script_search, multi_edit, search_game_tree, inspect_instance, search_asset, insert_asset, screen_capture, user_mouse_input, user_keyboard_input, character_navigation and subagent. Tip: call list_roblox_studios each session, because the studio id changes after a restart.
B22: Three core instances. InputContext groups actions and has Enabled, Priority and Sink. InputAction is one logical action with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition. InputBinding maps hardware to the action: KeyCode (keyboard, mouse or gamepad), UIButton for an on-screen touch button, and modifiers or composite directions. They're nested InputContext > InputAction > InputBinding. A Bool action signals a press with InputAction.Pressed and Released, StateChanged(newState) fires when the value changes, and you can poll GetState() (for analog input, poll every frame). Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in their own InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay or default player-script contexts, and enable Sink so inputs it consumes don't reach lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens and disable it on close, or disable the gameplay context. With Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem on, the default character controls also run as InputContexts, so a higher-priority sinking menu context overrides movement and jump.
B23: It's Roblox's UI styling system, like CSS for GuiObjects. The instances: StyleSheet is a collection of rules (and also works as a token or theme sheet). StyleRule has a Selector (class name like 'TextButton', a '.tag' from CollectionService, '#Name', states like ':hover', pseudo/child selectors) and properties set with SetProperty or SetProperties, plus Priority. StyleDerive lets a sheet inherit or derive from another sheet. StyleLink connects a StyleSheet to a UI tree: parent it under a ScreenGui (or other root) and point its StyleSheet at the sheet, and its rules then apply to matching descendants. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect or input type, like media queries). How styles reach the UI: StyleLink in the tree, then the sheet's rules match by selector and set properties, with more specific or higher-priority rules winning and explicitly set properties possibly conflicting (don't set the same property from both code and a style). Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (for example Primary = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim), reference them in rules as '$Primary', and share them through StyleDerive. Theming means swapping token sheets with the same names at runtime. The Style Editor is still in beta.
B24: Roblox requires an age check (facial age estimation through the app's camera, processed by a vendor, with ID verification or parental controls as a fallback or correction) to use chat. Users are placed into age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+. By default, users can chat only with their own group and the neighbouring groups (for example a 13-15 can chat with 9-12, 13-15 and 16-17), so children and adults can't chat freely. Under-9s have chat off by default unless a parent consents. Trusted Connections let age-checked 13+ users chat more widely with people they know. Users without an age check don't get chat. For developers: chat may not appear for some players, so don't make gameplay depend on typing, and there is no API exposing a player's age group.
